iCode: From Plan to Program

Year 6, Lesson 4

steps.label: Today's Task
steps.content:
Today's Task

Last lesson you planned your own game. Today you start building it for real.

  • Objective: program an algorithm according to a plan.
  • Success criteria: begin to program a game you have planned.

Key vocabulary

Algorithm; plan; sprite; costume; variable; iteration (repeat, forever, while); test; bug.

steps.label: From Plan to Code
steps.content:
From Plan to Code

Today you use the plan you wrote last lesson to start putting the code together for your game.

  • Start by importing, editing, or drawing the sprites your game needs.
  • Add the blocks of code needed to make them move.
  • Test your code as you go along - do not wait until everything is built.

Why test as you go?

Testing in a systematic way, a little bit at a time, is what real programmers do - it makes it much easier to find out exactly what is wrong when something breaks.

steps.label: Find Your Plan
steps.content:
Find Your Plan

You will need your plan from last lesson open while you work.

Before you start coding

  1. Go to the Lessons menu and open 6.2.3: iPlan.
  2. Go to the Review Your Plan slide near the end - everything you wrote last lesson is there.
  3. Keep that tab or window open so you can check back as you build.

A developer builds from a plan, not from memory - if you cannot remember a detail, go and check it.

items.prompt: What is a costume, in Scratch?
options: A different look or image for a sprite
A named place that stores a value that can change
items.explain: A sprite can have several costumes - switching costume is how you make it look like it is flying, walking, or has changed in some way.

items.prompt: Which of these is an example of a variable, not a sprite?
items.explain: score is a named place that stores a value that changes while the game runs - that makes it a variable, not a sprite.

steps.label: Getting Around in TurboWarp
steps.content:
Getting Around in TurboWarp

Before you start, make sure you know where everything is.

  • Block categories (left) - Motion is where you will find move, turn, and glide blocks.
  • Script area (middle) - drag blocks here and snap them together.
  • Stage and sprite list (right) - see your game and switch between sprites.

steps.label: Activity 1: Import or Draw Your Sprites
steps.content:
Activity 1: Import or Draw Your Sprites

Work independently - use your plan to build the sprites your game needs.

  1. Open your saved project in TurboWarp using the button.
  2. For each sprite on your plan: import a ready-made one, edit one, or draw your own.
  3. Import or edit any costume changes that sprite needs.
  4. Remind yourself: set the sprite's costume centre in the paint editor, so it can rotate correctly later.

The Slides and TurboWarp switcher stays at the top right - use it whenever you need the next instruction.

Before moving on

You should have every sprite from your plan added, with any costume changes it needs.

steps.label: Program Movement
steps.content:
Program Movement

Here is the real movement code from Fly High!, the example game from last lesson. Yours will not look identical, but the same ideas apply.

when green flag clicked
glide (1) secs to x: (-184) y: (-93)
point in direction (90)
ask [What angle, from my beak, should I fly at?] and wait
turn ccw (answer) degrees
repeat until <touching [edge v]?> or <touching [Pig v]?>
move (3) steps
end

Notice the pattern: get into a starting position, decide how to move, then keep moving until something makes it stop.

steps.label: Top Tip: Costume Centre
steps.content:
Top Tip: Costume Centre

Easy to miss, and it causes a real bug if you skip it.

Set the costume centre

In the paint editor, every costume has a centre point - the point it rotates and glides around. If it is in the wrong place, your sprite will spin or jump strangely instead of turning or moving smoothly.

  • Open a costume in the paint editor.
  • Use the costume centre tool to move the centre to the middle of the sprite.
  • Do this for every costume that sprite has.

steps.label: Activity 2: Program Your Sprites to Move
steps.content:
Activity 2: Program Your Sprites to Move

Work independently - add the blocks of code your plan needs for movement.

  1. For each sprite, add the blocks needed to move it the way your plan describes.
  2. Test after every small change - click the green flag and check it does what you expected.
  3. If something is wrong, that is a bug - fix it before adding the next piece of code.

The Slides and TurboWarp switcher stays at the top right - use it whenever you need the next instruction.

Before moving on

Every sprite you have added should move at least a little when you click the green flag.

steps.label: Easier and Harder
steps.content:
Easier and Harder

EasierImport ready-made sprites from the assets folder instead of drawing your own.
HarderAdd more "baddies" the higher the score gets - that means more sprites and more costume changes to manage.

steps.label: Testing Your Code
steps.content:
Testing Your Code

Look back at what you actually built today, then answer honestly - this is marked by you, not a computer.

items.prompt: Describe one bug you found while testing today, and what you think caused it (or, if you have not found one yet, what you will watch out for).
items.modelAnswer: A good answer names something specific that went wrong (for example: the sprite spun instead of moving, or moved the wrong direction) and links it to a real cause (for example: the costume centre was not set, or the wrong direction was used in a move/turn block) - not just "it didn't work".

items.prompt: Why should you test after adding each small piece of code, rather than waiting until the whole game is finished?
items.modelAnswer: If you only test at the end and something is wrong, it could be caused by any of the blocks you added - you have to check all of them. Testing after each small change means that if something breaks, you already know it must be the piece you just added, so bugs are much faster to find.
